summary: A 1979 specification of the Internet Message Protocol, a proposal for how messages are moved between hosts. It was written by Jon Postel and is part of the early work on internet mail. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 753 describes how mail systems on different networks can pass messages between one another. It gives messages a shared structure and has Message Processing Modules route them toward recipients.

questions: what is the internet message protocol
subtitle: A message format and routing protocol for mail moving between networks.

tldr.problem: Separate networks use different mail systems, so messages need a shared way to cross network boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: Message Processing Modules exchange structured messages, choose the next destination from routing information, and convert formats when local systems differ.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies a general internetwork message system, including message structure, commands, routing, and interfaces.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 753's status as Unknown. The document presents its message system as a specification intended to support compatible implementations.

sections.title: A Shared System for Network Mail
sections.content:
RFC 753 defines an Internet Message Protocol for transmitting messages between message processing modules (MPMs), processes that run on hosts. Together, MPMs form a delivery system across interconnected networks.

The protocol focuses on the internal transfer of messages rather than the user interface. It can carry text and structured data such as drawings, facsimile images, or digitized speech.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks can use one shared set of rules to exchange messages. The rules describe how systems pass messages, not how people write or read them.

sections.title: Message Parts and Data Elements
sections.content:
A message has an identification part, a command part, and a document part. Identification names the transaction and originating host; the command carries delivery instructions and a record of MPMs that handled it; the document contains a header and body.

Typed data elements provide the building blocks, including booleans, integers, bit strings, text, lists, and property lists. A message bag can group messages, and complete command or document parts can be shared by referring to an earlier message in that bag.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message separates its tracking information, delivery instructions, and content. The format uses basic types such as text, numbers, and lists to represent those parts.

sections.title: Routing and Delivery Between MPMs
sections.content:
An MPM examines queued messages and uses routing information to choose where they go. It can deliver to a user on its own host, send to another host on the same network, or forward to an MPM that is closer to a destination on another network.

Each MPM adds its identifier to the message stamp so other MPMs can detect a routing loop. MPMs exchange requests and replies, including delivery acknowledgments; the RFC expects a reliable two-way communication service, with TCP given as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: An MPM either delivers a message locally or forwards it to another MPM. Each one records that it handled the message, which helps reveal a message sent around in a loop.

sections.title: Working with Different Local Mail Systems
sections.content:
A network may keep using its own local mail system. A conversion program can translate outgoing local messages into the Internet format and translate incoming messages back into the local format.

The RFC warns that conversion can lose information when a local system cannot represent a feature. For example, a text-only system may replace speech in a message with a note that speech was present. The specification recommends delaying or avoiding such loss where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways can translate between the shared message format and a network's local format. A translation may lose details if the local system cannot represent them.
